records.our_prose: Habanero is a moderate feeder, and over its long season the timing matters more than the amount. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet, or a few inches of compost, into the bed before transplanting. Then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting and again once the first pods have set; Clemson suggests calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as the side-dress. The cardinal rule is to go easy on nitrogen: too much gives a big, bushy, leafy plant with few blooms and little fruit, the most common pepper-feeding mistake. Pair modest feeding with steady moisture, since even watering, not extra fertilizer, is what fills clean pods and heads off blossom-end rot.

records.our_prose: Harden off habanero transplants over 7 to 10 days, easing plants into sun and wind, and set them out only once the danger of frost is past, nights hold above 55°F, and the soil has warmed to at least 65°F. NC State advises planting Capsicum chinense only when nighttime temperatures are at least 55°F. Peppers set into cold ground simply sit and sulk, and habanero, a tropical species with a long season already, can least afford weeks lost to a cold start, so it is better to wait a week or two past the tomato date than to plant early into cold soil.

records.our_prose: A healthy habanero plant is prolific, setting dozens of small pods over its long season, far more numerous (though much smaller) than the six to eight fruit a bell pepper yields. Extension gives general pepper yields around 15 to 20 pounds per 10-foot row under good management; because habanero pods are small, a single plant can produce a large count of pods and, dried and ground, a good quantity of fiery powder. Steady warmth, even moisture, modest nitrogen, a long runway to ripen, and regular picking carry a plant to the upper end.
